rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope with all other settings fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. The initial elution window suggests this should retain all eight peaks without a large time penalty.

Keep the successful shallow slope and raise temperature to test selectivity for the remaining near-coeluting pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, creating room for further slope refinement if needed.

A small temperature reduction should move the remaining critical pair apart, while a slightly shallower gradient provides additional resolution margin. The last peak should still elute within 10 minutes.

Test a slightly shallower gradient at the best-performing temperature to improve the late critical pair. Comparing directly with injections 3 and 4 will show whether 60 C preserves sufficient separation in the earlier cluster.
The late critical pair improves with a steeper gradient at 60 C, so shorten tG to target R above 1.5. This also reduces retention time, though the earlier cluster may approach its resolution limit.

Injection 6 is nearly fully resolved; modestly raise the starting organic fraction to adjust selectivity while slightly flattening the gradient. This tests whether the early critical pair can reach R = 1.5 without sacrificing the late pair.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to lift both early critical pairs toward R = 1.5 while preserving the late pair's resolution margin. The lower endpoint remains well above the observed elution window.

Reduce the slope slightly to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting full resolution of both early critical pairs while retaining the late pair's margin. The endpoint remains above the last peak's estimated elution composition.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter elution window by raising phi0 while slightly reducing slope to protect the early critical pairs. This may shorten the last-peak time while retaining full resolution.

Lengthen injection 10's gradient by one step to recover separation of its early critical pair while retaining the shorter elution window. This tests whether full resolution is possible at phi0 = 0.15; injection 9 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Injection 9 already achieves the maximum score, while local slope changes at higher phi0 trade one unresolved pair for another. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a moderately steep gradient to seek a different fully resolved, sub-10-minute separation.

Raise temperature one step while keeping the gradient fixed to test whether the low-temperature critical pair separates. This should shorten retention, but the late pair with R = 1.65 will need monitoring.

Test a shallower gradient at 25 C to spread the crowded middle pair, with a higher starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved maximum-score method.

The low-temperature middle pair improved with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further while raising phi0 to limit retention time. This seeks a second fully resolved method with more resolution margin than injection 9.

Raise the starting and ending fractions together to preserve slope while shortening the fully resolved low-temperature separation. This isolates the effect of the starting composition on the critical middle pair.

The middle pair converged strongly when phi0 increased, suggesting a possible elution-order crossover. Test beyond that crossover at the same slope to seek renewed separation and a substantially shorter run, retaining injection 9 as the best method.

Injection 17 is fully resolved with useful margin, so steepen the gradient to shorten its 4.98-minute separation. Keep temperature and starting composition fixed to isolate the speed–resolution tradeoff.
Shorten the gradient one more step while holding selectivity settings fixed. Injection 18's minimum R of 1.79 suggests some remaining room to reduce elution time without losing full resolution.
Test the next shorter gradient to locate the full-resolution speed limit. The middle pair is likely to fall below R = 1.5, in which case injection 19 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature one step to seek a shorter separation through temperature-dependent selectivity. Monitor the middle critical pair closely; injection 19 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Test beyond the apparent temperature-driven crossover of the middle critical pair to seek renewed resolution at shorter retention times. Injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
Return to 25 C and test a higher starting fraction with a shallower slope to seek faster elution while protecting the middle cluster. Injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 19's gradient to just beyond the observed elution window while preserving its successful slope and temperature. This should retain full resolution and the approximately 4.14-minute last-peak time with a much shorter programmed gradient.

Use the final injection to test a slope between the fastest fully resolved method and injection 20, seeking a shorter separation near the resolution boundary. If the middle pair falls below R = 1.5, retain injection 24, which achieves CRF 1.000 with the last peak at 4.14 minutes.
